title: MZ A Fun Dive into the "Invisible Monster" Design

posts.author: Muharukahana_Studio
posts.body:
Alright, let’s talk about this super cool "invisible monster" I cooked up for my game! Originally, it was meant to be a gnarly, blood-soaked creature, but making walking sprites was a total nightmare. So, I brainstormed and landed on something wild: a monster with no physical form, entirely driven by a state machine. No sprite, just pure mechanics messing with the player’s head!
This monster has three forms—
Student
,
Janitor
, and
Waiter（actually w**re in game）
—and it switches between them based on the player’s actions every few seconds, counted as one action turn. The Waiter only shows up later in the story, adding a spicy twist.
Since pasting images is a hassle, I’ll paint the picture with words. The game’s set in a hotel-like map where players solve puzzles and explore, zipping between corridors and rooms. That’s the main stage for this chapter.
Student Morph​
When the player’s chilling in a room, the monster’s in Student mode, prowling outside the hotel. Picture it draped in chains and books, clanking like a walking library. Every time the player makes noise—like smashing a plate or interacting with stuff (adding to the "whisper value")—the monster zeroes in. There’s a "distance value" (0 is in-your-face, 9 is far off) that shifts constantly. If the player makes noise, the monster tries knocking on a door. If it’s super close (distance 0), it bangs on
your
room’s door, cue the jump scare!
Janitor Morph​
Try leaving the room, and the mess you made inside (tracked as "dirtiness value") gets locked in. That triggers the Janitor morph. The dirtier you are, the faster this guy closes the distance, like a cleaning fanatic on your tail! But if you duck back into a room, it switches to Student mode. If the monster catches you (distance 0) and you’ve got a light on—room lamp or handheld—it gets spooked, adding to its "fear-of-light value." Once that value maxes out, the monster stops fearing light and flips to Waiter mode.
Oh, and here’s a kicker: if the Student knocks on your room’s door while you’re inside, it also turns into the Waiter.
Waiter(*****) Morph​
The Waiter is
intense
. It knocks on doors like it’s demanding room service, whether you’re in a room or not, and it doesn’t care about your whisper value. Catch probability skyrockets! If you’re outside, it closes the distance, but unlike the Janitor, the dirtier you are, the
slower
it moves. And yeah, it’s immune to light now.
If a room you dirtied up has trash, the next turn flips the monster to Janitor mode, whether you’re inside or out. The Janitor keeps closing in but doesn’t knock, so you’re safe in a room even if the distance is low. When it switches back to Student, it uses the Janitor’s close distance as a starting point. Also, if you leave a room while the monster’s a Student, it stays Student until the next turn, giving you a brief "safe window" before the Janitor kicks in.
Deep Dive: Student Morph Approach Mechanics​
The Student’s approach is the trickiest part, driven by two random numbers:
Move Direction
: 1 or else（most 2）
Move Distance
: 1 unit, 2 units,  3 units (only distance wall).
After rolling these, the monster’s state gets processed. I set up "distance walls":
At distance 0 (too close), it’s forced to move 3 units away, direction locked to "away," no random roll.
At distance 9 (too far), it moves 3 units closer, direction locked to "approach."
This keeps things controlled. The monster tends to hover in a range, not moving consistently, probably because RPG Maker MZ’s random number system isn’t as jumpy as Perlin noise. Even with refreshes, it feels sticky. So, I added a "lockdown value" to track how long it lingers in a distance range. There’s an approach lockdown (distances 0-2, cap 3) and an away lockdown (7-9, cap 2). Hit the cap, and it’s forced to distance 5. These are separate counters to avoid conflicts. By tweaking lockdown and move distance, I can make the monster pop up more or less often, creating a "feels random but kinda predictable" vibe. Since each turn is like 30-60 seconds, even frequent encounters don’t feel annoying—they’re challenging and fun!
Picture this: you’re sneaking through puzzles in Student mode, accidentally smash a plate (whisper value spikes), and realize the monster’s closing in. You bolt out of the room, and next turn, it’s a Janitor, hot on your heels, shrinking the distance fast. You duck into another room, but it’s not always safe—those lockdown and wall mechanics keep things spicy but fair. This setup gives players freedom to puzzle-solve (no other characters on the map!) while the invisible monster keeps them paranoid. They can’t fully crack the state machine, so they lean on plot hints ("correct info") to dodge it.
The Fun Part: Outsmarting the Monster​
You might think players are just sitting ducks, but the three-morph cycle flips that. Let’s break it down:
State Machine
: Morphs switch based on player actions every few seconds, so players can time their moves to mess with it.
Student
: Wanders, knocks on noise, hits your door and becomes Waiter. Sets distance.
Janitor
: Always chases, faster with higher dirtiness, fears light until it doesn’t, then turns Waiter.
Waiter
: Knocks constantly, chases slower with higher dirtiness. Trash in a room flips it to Janitor next turn.
Imagine this: you use the Janitor to spook it with light, then slip into a room to push the distance out. In Student mode, if the distance is far (say, 6-9), you’ve got time to puzzle without worrying about noise. If it gets close and knocks, it turns Waiter. You make yourself super dirty, leave trash in the room, and when the Waiter barges in, the next turn it’s a Janitor. Since you’re filthy, the Waiter was slow chasing you outside, and by the time it’s a Janitor, you’re back in a room, forcing it to Student mode. Now you’re not just running scared—you’re
toying
with the monster! Players can use known info to bait morph switches, playing a cat-and-mouse game. Each dodge feels like a win, turning fear into a rush of outsmarting death.
Welcome to provide feedback.
